title: Current and potential difference — the basics of every circuit
examTip: Questions using Q = It, E = QV and R = V/I come up almost every year. I-V characteristics are a favourite for 'describe and explain' questions, especially the filament lamp and diode. Examiners want the physics reason, not just the shape.
introTips: Current, potential difference and resistance: the three quantities in every circuit question
Equations: Q = I t, V = I R, E = Q V
You will sketch and explain I-V graphs and describe two required practicals
intro: Every electrical device you use runs on charge flowing round a circuit. Your phone, a kettle and a torch all depend on it. Current, potential difference and resistance let you predict how any circuit behaves. Get them right, and much of this topic becomes simple.

basics.text: Electric charge is what flows when electricity flows. In a metal wire, tiny charged particles can move along the wire. You cannot see charge, but you can see what it does, like lighting a bulb.
A circuit is a complete loop of wire that charge can flow round. It is like a running track: you end up back where you started. If there is a gap anywhere, nothing flows.
A cell is what pushes charge round a circuit. A battery is two or more cells joined together. It is a bit like a pump pushing water round a loop of pipe.
Energy is what is needed to make things happen. It makes things move, heat up, light up or make a sound. You cannot see energy, but you can see what it does.
A rate tells you how much happens each second. Speed is a rate: how many metres you travel each second.
Letters in an equation stand for quantities, such as t for time. Two letters written side by side are multiplied together. To use it, swap the letters for numbers.

basics.idea: The two axes of a graph
basics.text: A graph has a line across the bottom, called the x-axis. The line up the side is the y-axis. Each one shows a quantity you measured. Each point on the graph is one pair of readings.

The origin is the point on a graph where both quantities are zero. On many graphs it is the bottom-left corner. On some, the axes cross in the middle, and the origin is where they cross. A line "through the origin" means that when one quantity is zero, so is the other.

keyPoints.heading: Electric current — charge on the move
keyPoints.content:
Every torch, phone and kettle runs on something moving through its wires. Turn on a torch and the bulb lights at once. Inside the metal wire, tiny particles that carry <dfn>electric charge</dfn> start to drift round together. You cannot see charge, but you can see what it does.

A complete loop is a <dfn>closed circuit</dfn>. Charge only flows round a closed circuit if it includes something to push it, such as a cell or a battery. That push is called a <dfn>potential difference</dfn>, and the next key point explains it. Break the loop anywhere and the flow stops everywhere. A <dfn>switch</dfn> does this on purpose: it opens a gap in the loop.

A flow of charge is an <dfn>electric current</dfn>. Its size is the <dfn>rate</dfn> of flow: how much charge passes a point each second. Charge is counted in <dfn>coulombs</dfn> (C). Current is measured in <dfn>amperes</dfn> (A, or amps) with an <dfn>ammeter</dfn>. One ampere means one coulomb passing each second.

In a single loop, the current is the same at every point, because charge is not used up on the way round. So it does not matter where you put the ammeter.

The amount of charge that passes is the <dfn>charge flow</dfn>, Q. To find it, multiply the current by the time in seconds.

definitions: Electric current is a flow of electrical charge. Its size is the rate of flow of charge.

keyPoints.heading: Potential difference and resistance — push and opposition
keyPoints.content:
Connect a lamp to one cell and it glows dimly. Use two cells and it glows brighter, because more current flows. Put a <dfn>resistor</dfn>, a part that limits the current, in the loop as well. The lamp dims again, because less current flows. So the size of a current depends on two things.

A <dfn>component</dfn> is any part of a circuit, such as a lamp or a resistor. The first thing is the push that drives charge through the component: the potential difference across it. It is measured in <dfn>volts</dfn> (V) with a <dfn>voltmeter</dfn>, which is connected across the part you are testing. People often call it <dfn>voltage</dfn>. Exam questions say potential difference, but either word gets the mark.

The second is how hard the component makes it for charge to get through: its <dfn>resistance</dfn>. Resistance is measured in <dfn>ohms</dfn> (Ω). For the same potential difference, the bigger the resistance, the smaller the current.

The three are linked by one equation: potential difference equals current times resistance. If you know any two of them, you can rearrange it to find the third.
writeBullets: Potential difference (voltage) is the push, measured in volts with a voltmeter
Resistance opposes the current; it is measured in ohms (Ω)
Same potential difference, bigger resistance: smaller current

definitions: The current through a component depends on its resistance and on the potential difference across it.
For a fixed potential difference, a bigger resistance means a smaller current.

workedExamples.question: A potential difference of 6 V is put across a 12 Ω resistor. What is the current through it?

steps.text: Write the equation: V = I R.
You want I, so divide both sides by R: I = V ÷ R.

keyTerms.def: The push that makes charge flow through a component. Measured in volts (V). Also called voltage.
The unit of potential difference. 1 volt is 1 joule per coulomb.
Another name for potential difference.
A component that limits the current in a circuit.
A meter that measures potential difference. It is connected across a component.
How much a component opposes the current through it. Measured in ohms (Ω).
The unit of resistance. 1 ohm is 1 volt per ampere.
Any part of a circuit, such as a lamp, a resistor or a diode.

keyPoints.memTip: V = I R. To find I, divide V by R. To find R, divide V by I.

keyPoints.heading: Required practical — the resistance of a wire
keyPoints.content:
Heaters, leads and the coils inside motors all use wire, so engineers need to know how its length changes its resistance. You can measure it yourself.

In this required practical, a long wire is clipped along a metre ruler and connected to a cell. An ammeter goes in the loop, connected <dfn>in series</dfn>: one after another with the wire, so the same current flows through both. A voltmeter is connected across the wire, <dfn>in parallel</dfn> with it, to measure the potential difference. Then find the resistance: divide the potential difference by the current.

Move one clip to change the length, and repeat. Keep the current small and switch off between readings, so the wire does not warm up. That keeps it at a <dfn>constant temperature</dfn>, which means its temperature stays the same. You find that a longer wire has a bigger resistance.

The same circuit measures two or more resistors joined together, in series or in parallel. Measure the potential difference and the current for each combination, then find its resistance the same way.
keyPoints.diagramCaption: Measuring the resistance of a wire. Moving one clip changes the length being tested.
writeBullets: Ammeter in series with the wire; voltmeter in parallel across it
Resistance = potential difference ÷ current
At constant temperature, a longer wire has a bigger resistance

definitions: At constant temperature, the resistance of a wire increases as its length increases.
To find a resistance, measure the potential difference and the current, then use R = V ÷ I.

workedExamples.question: A length of the wire has a potential difference of 1.5 V across it and a current of 0.3 A through it. What is its resistance?

steps.text: You want R, so divide both sides by I: R = V ÷ I.

keyTerms.def: Connected one after another in the same loop, so the same current flows through each.
Connected side by side, across the same two points.
The temperature stays the same throughout the measurements.

keyPoints.memTip: L for Length, L for Larger: a longer wire has a larger resistance.

keyPoints.heading: Ohmic conductors — resistance that stays the same
keyPoints.content:
Some components behave in a simple, steady way. In others, the resistance changes as the current changes. To find out which is which, you measure the current through a component at several potential differences and plot a graph.

This graph is called an <dfn>I-V characteristic</dfn>. Current (I) goes up the side and potential difference (V) goes along the bottom. For a resistor kept at a constant temperature, the points lie on a straight line through the origin. Double the potential difference and the current doubles too. When two quantities change together like this, the current is <dfn>directly proportional</dfn> to the potential difference.

A straight line means the resistance is not changing as the current changes. A component that behaves this way is an <dfn>ohmic conductor</dfn>. Its resistance stays the same whatever the current, as long as its temperature does not change.

So for an ohmic conductor you can use V = I R with one fixed value of R.
keyPoints.diagramCaption: The I-V characteristic of a resistor at constant temperature.
writeBullets: I-V characteristic: current (up the side) against potential difference (along)
Ohmic conductor: a straight line through the origin
Current directly proportional to potential difference; resistance stays constant

definitions: For an ohmic conductor at constant temperature, the current is directly proportional to the potential difference.
So the resistance of an ohmic conductor stays constant as the current changes.

keyTerms.def: A graph of current (up the side) against potential difference (along the bottom) for a component.
When one quantity doubles, the other doubles too. The graph is a straight line through the origin.
A component whose resistance stays constant at constant temperature. Its I-V graph is a straight line through the origin.

keyPoints.memTip: Ohmic = Ordinary: a straight line, the same resistance all the way.

keyPoints.heading: Filament lamps and diodes — resistance that changes
keyPoints.content:
Not every component gives a straight line. Some give curves, and the shapes tell you what is happening inside them.

An old-style bulb is a <dfn>filament lamp</dfn>. It has a thin coil of metal wire, the filament, that glows white-hot. As the current rises, the filament gets hotter, and its resistance increases as its temperature increases. So each extra volt pushes through less extra current than the one before. The graph bends over and gets flatter.

A <dfn>diode</dfn> lets current flow in one direction only. Connect it one way round and current flows. Turn it round and almost nothing flows, because the diode has a very high resistance in the reverse direction. The graph lies flat along the axis on one side and rises steeply on the other.

For both components, the resistance is different at different points on the graph. To find it at one point, read off V and I there, then divide V by I.
keyPoints.diagramCaption: I-V graphs for a filament lamp and a diode.
writeBullets: Filament lamp: gets hotter, resistance increases, graph curves and flattens
Diode: current flows in one direction only
Diode: very high resistance in the reverse direction

definitions: As a filament lamp gets hotter, its resistance increases.
A diode lets current flow in one direction only. In the reverse direction its resistance is very high.
At any point on an I-V graph, resistance = potential difference ÷ current.

keyTerms.def: A bulb with a thin metal wire (the filament) that glows when hot. Its resistance increases as it gets hotter.
A component that lets current flow in one direction only. It has a very high resistance in the reverse direction.

keyPoints.memTip: Three shapes: straight line = resistor. Bending over = lamp (it gets hot). Flat one side, steep the other = diode (one way only).

keyPoints.heading: Required practical — measuring I-V characteristics
keyPoints.content:
Exam questions often ask you to describe how to get these graphs, so it is worth knowing the method step by step.

The circuit has a cell or battery and the component you are testing. An ammeter is in series with the component and a voltmeter is in parallel across it. A <dfn>variable resistor</dfn> (also called a rheostat), a resistor you can adjust with a slider, is in the loop too. Moving the slider changes the current, so you get a range of readings.

Start with the variable resistor at its highest resistance, so the current is small. Record the current and the potential difference, then move the slider and record again. Take repeat readings and find the mean. To get the other half of the graph, turn the component round and repeat; these readings count as negative. The lamp gets very hot, so do not touch it.

Test a resistor at constant temperature, a filament lamp and a diode, and plot current against potential difference for each. A straight-line graph means the component is <dfn>linear</dfn>; any other shape means it is <dfn>non-linear</dfn>. So a resistor at constant temperature is linear, and the filament lamp and the diode are non-linear. The shape shows how its resistance behaves, and so what the component is useful for. A diode, for example, can stop current flowing the wrong way.
keyPoints.diagramCaption: The circuit for measuring an I-V graph: ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel.
writeBullets: Ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel, variable resistor to change the current
Turn the component round to get negative readings
Resistor: linear. Filament lamp and diode: non-linear

definitions: To measure the resistance of a component: ammeter in series with it, voltmeter in parallel across it, a variable resistor to change the current.
A straight-line I-V graph is linear; any other shape is non-linear. The filament lamp and diode are non-linear.

keyTerms.def: A resistor whose resistance you can change, often with a slider. Used to change the current in a circuit.
Gives a straight-line graph.
Gives a graph that is not a straight line, such as the curve of a filament lamp or the graph of a diode.

keyPoints.memTip: Series A, Parallel V: Ammeter in Series, Voltmeter in Parallel. Cover your notes. Describe the full circuit from memory, including the safety step.

keyPoints.heading: Energy transferred — what the charge carries
keyPoints.content:
A cell does more than push charge round a circuit. It gives energy to the charge, and the charge hands that energy over in the components: lighting a lamp, warming a heater, turning a motor.

When charge flows through a component, <dfn>work is done</dfn>: energy is transferred from the charge to the component. Energy is measured in <dfn>joules</dfn> (J).

The potential difference across a component tells you how much energy each coulomb transfers there. A potential difference of 1 volt means 1 joule is transferred for each coulomb that passes. So 12 V means 12 joules for every coulomb.

To find the total <dfn>energy transferred</dfn>, multiply the charge flow by the potential difference. If you are given a current and a time instead of a charge, find the charge first with Q = I t.
writeBullets: When charge flows, work is done: energy is transferred
1 volt means 1 joule transferred per coulomb
Energy (J) = charge flow (C) × potential difference (V)

definitions: When charge flows through a component, work is done and energy is transferred.
A potential difference of 1 volt transfers 1 joule of energy per coulomb of charge.

equations.words: energy transferred = charge flow × potential difference

workedExamples.question: A heater has a potential difference of 12 V across it. A current of 2 A flows through it for 30 s. How much energy is transferred?

steps.text: First find the charge: Q = I t = 2 × 30 = 60 C.
Write the energy equation: E = Q V.

keyTerms.def: Energy transferred. Work is done when charge flows through a component.
The unit of energy.
The energy passed on as charge flows through a component, in joules (J).

keyPoints.memTip: E = QV: energy transferred = charge flow × potential difference. More charge or a bigger p.d. means more energy.

0.question: A current of 3 A flows through a lamp for 10 s. How much charge flows?
0.wrongFeedback: Use Q = I t: multiply the current by the time. 3 × 10 = 30 C.

1.question: A resistor has a potential difference of 12 V across it and a current of 2 A through it. What is its resistance?
1.wrongFeedback: Rearrange V = I R to R = V ÷ I. Then 12 ÷ 2 = 6 Ω. If you chose 24 Ω, you multiplied instead of dividing.

2.question: In the resistance of a wire practical, the temperature stays constant. What happens to the resistance when you test a longer piece of the wire?
2.correctFeedback: Correct. At constant temperature, a longer wire has a bigger resistance.
2.wrongFeedback: At constant temperature, the resistance of a wire increases as its length increases.

3.question: What does the I-V characteristic of a resistor at constant temperature look like?
options: A straight line through the origin
Flat on one side, steep on the other
A flat line along the bottom
3.correctFeedback: Correct. It is an ohmic conductor: current is directly proportional to potential difference, so the line is straight through the origin.
3.wrongFeedback: A resistor at constant temperature is an ohmic conductor. Its resistance stays the same, so the graph is a straight line through the origin.

4.question: Why does the I-V graph of a filament lamp curve instead of being straight?
options: The lamp lets current flow in one direction only
As the current rises, the filament gets hotter and its resistance increases
The potential difference falls as the current rises
The ammeter reads wrongly at high currents
4.correctFeedback: Exactly right. The hotter filament has a bigger resistance, so each extra volt adds less current. The line bends over.
4.wrongFeedback: Think about temperature. More current makes the filament hotter, and a hotter filament has more resistance. So the current rises less and less, and the graph curves.

5.question: In the I-V practical, how are the ammeter and voltmeter connected?
options: Ammeter in series with the component, voltmeter in parallel across it
Both in series with the component
Both in parallel across the component
Ammeter in parallel, voltmeter in series
5.correctFeedback: Correct. The ammeter is in series to measure the current through the component. The voltmeter is in parallel to measure the potential difference across it.
5.wrongFeedback: The ammeter must be in series, so the same current flows through it and the component. The voltmeter must be in parallel, to measure the potential difference across the component.

6.question: A charge of 5 C flows through a potential difference of 12 V. How much energy is transferred?
6.wrongFeedback: Use E = Q V: multiply the charge flow by the potential difference. 5 × 12 = 60 J.

commonMistakes: Drawing the filament lamp I-V curve bending towards the I-axis instead of away from it. It curves away because resistance increases, so less current flows than expected.
Connecting the voltmeter in series instead of parallel. A voltmeter must be in parallel, across the component, to measure the potential difference across it.
Forgetting to check units in Q = It. Time must be in seconds, not minutes or hours, before substituting.
Saying a diode 'blocks all current' in the reverse direction. It has a very high resistance, so a very small current flows.
examTips: Always show the formula, then the substitution, then the answer with units. Even one mark is at stake if you skip a step.

For 'describe and explain' I-V questions, name the shape and then explain the physics. For example: 'The curve means resistance is increasing, because the filament temperature rises as current increases'.

In the required practical, know why each meter goes where it does. Don't just say 'ammeter = series, voltmeter = parallel'. Give the reason. The ammeter measures the current through the component. The voltmeter measures the p.d. across it.
Current is only directly proportional to potential difference for an ohmic conductor at constant temperature. Don't assume this for lamps or diodes.
